definition: Pristine means in its original, unspoiled condition.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pristine. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pristine should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: She returned the borrowed telescope pristine, without so much as a fingerprint on the brass.

Clean says only that today's dirt is gone — a scrubbed counter is clean by suppertime and smudged by dawn; it claims far less than pristine, which asks whether the thing is still in its original state, dirt and all.

Spotless goes further than clean: not one mark anywhere, however hard you look — but a thing can be spotless and much-used; pristine claims the most, the original condition itself, as if nothing had ever happened to it.

Unspoiled means nothing has damaged or cheapened it — the word rules out harm and stops there. Pristine makes the larger claim of original condition: not merely unharmed but unchanged since the beginning, nothing altered, nothing updated.

Untouched means no hand has been laid on it at all — a claim about contact, not condition. A borrowed telescope can come home pristine, used but exactly as it began; untouched would mean nobody had ever picked it up.
worn and marked by use and the elements
its original condition ruined past recovery

Pristinus is the only word Latin sent us from this stem, so pristine has no everyday relatives. Its old parent, prius ("before"), does stand behind prior and prime — pristine is the "before" state of a thing, carried unspoiled into the present — but that kinship is a family legend, not a root you can peel off and reuse.
Pristine means in its original, unspoiled condition.
The expedition hut has been locked against the weather since 1912, and the room inside is pristine — stepping in is stepping into the sentence the men never finished.
Tins of cocoa stand in ranks on the shelf.
Socks hang stiff on a line above the stove.
A magazine lies open, face down, keeping someone's place.
Conservators enter a few days each summer, count everything, touch almost nothing, and lock the door again.
Pristine is the exact word for that room, because it means in its original, unspoiled condition.
Nothing about the hut is clean — a century of soot films every surface — but nothing has been moved, mended, or modernized.
Original is the claim pristine makes; a scrubbed and rebuilt hut would be tidier, and would have lost the very thing the word names.
Pristine makes a stronger claim than clean: original and unspoiled, as if time and use had never touched the thing.
Ads have blurred it toward "very tidy," but the exact sense is worth keeping — a spotless kitchen has been wiped; a pristine wilderness has never needed wiping.
For surfaces, spotless; for landscapes, relics, and first editions, pristine.

In 2017, a survey ship mapping the Black Sea floor spotted an ancient Greek trading vessel more than a mile down.
Marine archaeologists date the wreck to 400 B.C., yet its mast still stands, and the rowing benches and rudder sit exactly where the builders fitted them.
The secret is the deep water itself: below a certain depth the Black Sea holds no oxygen, so the shipworms that devour sunken timber cannot live there.
Researchers called the ship pristine, and few wrecks anywhere have earned the word — twenty-four centuries have passed, and nothing about the vessel has changed.
A museum copy could show us the design; only this hull can show us the very wood the builders handled.
